claims.text: The superconducting transition temperature of a fully disordered high-entropy alloy is primarily governed by its average valence electron count.
Average valence electron count controls the electronic density of states at the Fermi level.
Average valence electron count controls the strength of electron–phonon coupling.
Average valence electron count is a composition-dependent alloy descriptor that may be adjusted through elemental substitution.
Replacing some Nb or Ta with Ti will change the average valence electron count of the proposed alloy.
A fully disordered, single-phase, Nb–Ta-dominated alloy can serve as the starting material while satisfying the requirement of at least five elements at no less than 5 atomic percent each.
Arc melting followed by homogenization will ensure a uniform, single-phase microstructure.
Holding processing conditions, temperature, pressure, and phase homogeneity constant provides a controlled comparison between the baseline and VEC-modified alloys.
There is an optimal valence electron count at which electron–phonon coupling is enhanced.
Enhanced electron–phonon coupling promotes Cooper-pair formation and increases the superconducting transition temperature.
Deviation from the optimal electron count increases disorder scattering.
Increased disorder scattering reduces the superconducting transition temperature.
Alloys tuned closer to the optimal valence electron count will have a higher transition temperature than the baseline Nb–Ta alloy.
Alloys tuned away from the optimal valence electron count will have a lower transition temperature than the baseline.
Secondary-phase formation or significant chemical segregation may invalidate the proposed VEC–superconductivity relationship.

The hypothesis is falsified if systematic VEC variation produces no consistent or predictable correlation with transition temperature, including no peak or an invariant transition temperature despite measured electronic-structure changes.

contradictions.description: The baseline is called 'as-cast' while also being described as subject to identical homogenization heat-treatment conditions. An as-cast baseline and a homogenized baseline are not the same material state unless the sequence is clarified.
